definition: Bombastic means using inflated, self-important language with little substance.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word bombastic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know bombastic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The gym's bombastic radio spot promised 'a total rebirth of the human body'; the gym itself contained one treadmill and two mirrors.
A showy phrase wants attention but can still be honest about its size — far milder than bombastic, which inflates the claim itself.
Flowery language piles on ornament, yet it stops short of bombastic: flowers decorate a real message, while bombast replaces the message with hot air.

Overblown means puffed past its true size — the claim, the ceremony, or the reaction is bigger than the facts beneath it, whether or not anyone is showing off. Bombastic is narrower: overblown language specifically, self-important wording with nothing solid inside. A forecast can be overblown; only speech and writing can be bombastic.

Pompous describes a person's whole self-important manner — the bearing, the tone, the certainty of one's own importance. Bombastic points at the language alone: a modest-mannered writer can still produce bombastic prose, and a pompous man can speak in perfectly plain words. Judge the person pompous, the wording bombastic.

Grandiloquent language reaches for lofty, high-flown words — the style is grand whether or not anything real sits underneath it. Bombastic adds the hollowness: it is grandiloquence with nothing inside, all inflation and no substance. A grandiloquent speech can carry a genuine argument; a bombastic one, by definition, cannot.

The awards-show host grew more bombastic with every category: by midnight he was introducing a regional jingle contest as 'a turning point in the history of sound itself.'

Bombastic is more precise than 'exaggerated' or 'wordy' because it points at inflated, self-important language with nothing solid inside — the verbal equivalent of padding, all stuffing and no substance.
Use bombastic to mock language that inflates itself — campaign promises, trailer voice-overs.
Plain 'exaggerated' overstates facts; bombastic overdresses them.
Its unit-mates mark the poles: laconic speech barely opens its mouth, prosaic speech is flat but honest, and bombastic speech booms about nothing.

The launch was scheduled for noon, but first the founder wanted to talk, and the talking did not stop.
For fifty minutes he paced the stage promising 'the rebirth of human connection' and 'a leap past every limit of the modern mind,' while the device sat under its velvet cloth.
Reporters transcribing the speech found it bombastic in the precise sense: enormous words arranged around no checkable claim, inflation with nothing solid inside.

One veteran reviewer summed up the morning in her notebook: 'Fifty minutes of thunder, four ounces of plastic.'
